newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EBRD wants new Marshall Plan for ex-Soviet Union.
newsitem.headline: EBRD wants new Marshall Plan for ex-Soviet Union.

text.p: A leading official of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) appealed on Thursday for a new Marshall Plan to tackle poverty and pollution in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

"Transition has been very unequal among various countries amd remains subject to slippages and accidents," Bernard Snoy, EBRD Director for Belgium, Luxembourg and Slovenia told a conference in Budapest marking the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan that helped rebuild Europe after World War Two.

"Whereas (in Central Europe) access to private capital flows or to existing international financial institutions eliminates the need for new concessional facilities, the remaining areas where I see a strong case for a type of Marshall Two plan...are the CIS countries," he said.
"An uncertain investment climate, deficiencies of taxation systems, crime and corruption have discouraged domestic and foreign investment."

Snoy said that in most of the former Soviet Union, capital flight was continuing at high levels, the social situation remained alarming and pressing environment problems, particularly those related to nuclear safety, remained unresolved.

"Stronger social support programmes are needed to alleviate poverty and make reforms politically and socially sustainable in the CIS countries where social indicators point to a dramatic decline in standards of living of large segments of the population," he said.
Snoy said recent events in Albania showed that apparent reforms could easily be reversed if conditions for ordinary people worsened.
"The tragic events in Albania are an illustration of how hard-won progress in transition can be lost with frightening speed," he said.
Western funds were also needed to reduce environmental pollution, reform the energy sector and most importantly, promote nuclear safety.
"Action by the G7 (the seven most developed economies) has concentrated on the closure of the Chernobyl reactors which are only a few among the many more dangerous reactors in activity," he said.
Chernobyl, in Ukraine, was the scene of the world's worst nuclear accident in 1986 when a reactor meltdown killed over 100 people and leaked radiation over a wide area.

The three-day conference entitled Corporate Governance, Financial Markets and Global Convergence, which began on Thursday, was organised by the European University Society for Financial Research (SUERF) and the Robert Triffin-Szirak Foundation.
